stories.title: On, Sneaker Maker Beloved by Roger Federer and Kylian Mbappé, Moves HQ to Penn 1
stories.excerpt: It’s On! The Swiss athletic sneaker and apparel company now known as On is moving and expanding its New York City office headquarters to 85,000 square feet at Vornado Realty Trust’s Penn 1, Commercial Observer has learned. The company, previously known as On Running, is currently located in a small office by comparison at Spear Street Capital’s 165 Mercer Street in SoHo. According to industry sources, On will have 61,000 square feet on the entire eighth floor of Midtown’s 1 Pennsylvania Plaza, as well as 24,000 square feet on part of the seventh floor, where the company will enjoy an outdoor terrace. The 15-year deal had an asking rent of $120 per square foot. A CBRE team of Sinclair Li, Patrick Moroney and Liz Lash represented On in the deal, while Vornado was repped in-house by a team of Jared Silverman and Josh Glick. The company was founded in the Swiss Alps in 2010 by Ironman champion Olivier Bernhard. He later brought in friends Caspar Coppetti and David Allemann, now co-CEOs, to form the company. By 2012, Swiss triathlete Nicola Spirig was wearing the brand’s Cloudracer shoe, and sales took off. Tennis star Roger Federer became a shareholder in November 2019, and the company released a shoe called the “Roger” in July 2020. It went public in September 2021 on the New York Stock Exchange, raising $746 million. On is growing its direct-to-consumer sales and has a mission “to ignite the human spirit through movement” by selling “premium footwear, apparel and accessories for high performance running, outdoor, training, all-day activities and tennis,” according to its website. On’s tagline — “dream on” — is resonating with consumers in over 90 countries, with sales reaching $1 billion in the second quarter of this year, up by 13.5 percent year-over-year with a gross profit of $676 million. In mid-September, French soccer star Kylian Mbappé even ditched Nike and became On’s global ambassador. On already has New York City stores at 162 Fifth Avenue in the Flatiron Di
bullets: On (Swiss sneaker brand) expands NYC HQ to 85,000 SF at Penn 1 (Midtown Manhattan)
Relocates from 165 Mercer Street (SoHo) to larger Vornado space, signals office demand recovery
CBRE brokered deal; founder Olivier Bernhard scaled brand from 2010 Swiss startup to major employer
stories.summary: On, the Swiss athletic apparel company, is expanding its New York City headquarters from a smaller SoHo office to 85,000 square feet across the 7th and 8th floors of Penn 1 in Midtown Manhattan. The company occupies 61,000 SF on the full 8th floor plus 24,000 SF on the 7th floor with an outdoor terrace. The deal signals strong tenant demand for premium office space in Manhattan's Midtown market and represents confidence in NYC as a corporate hub for growth-stage consumer brands.
stories.impact: Office absorption in Midtown Manhattan from mid-market growth companies demonstrates selective recovery in trophy office; this occupancy pull does not translate to multifamily demand directly, though co-location of high-wage tech and consumer-brand employees in Midtown may support rental demand in adjacent residential submarkets (Murray Hill, Kips Bay) if On's hiring accelerates.

stories.title: TA Realty Pays $105M for Wellington Rental Community
stories.excerpt: JPMorgan Investment Management sold The Polo Lakes Apartments in Wellington for more than twice what it paid. The South Florida Business Journal reports JP Morgan paid $47.75 million for the property in 2002. TA Realty paid $105.45 million for the same 366-unit rental community in 2026. Totaling 520,918 square feet, Polo Lakes was built on the 19.2-acre site in 2000. It includes a pool, clubhouse, tennis court, and basketball court. Polo Lakes units range from 795 to 1,554 square feet and rent from $1,974 to $5,341. This is its largest apartment deal in South Florida since it acquired an apartment complex in Pembroke Pines for $118 million in early 2025. Founded in 1982, TA Realty has over $19 billion of total assets under management. The post TA Realty Pays $105M for Wellington Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: TA Realty acquires Polo Lakes (366 units, Wellington, FL) for $105.45M—$47.75M in 2002 shows strong appreciation
Rents $1,974–$5,341/mo across 795–1,554 SF units; property built 2000 on 19.2 acres with full amenities
TA Realty's second major South Florida deal in 12 months ($118M Pembroke Pines, early 2025); AUM $19B
stories.summary: TA Realty paid $105.45 million for The Polo Lakes Apartments, a 366-unit community in Wellington, Florida, acquired by previous owner JPMorgan Investment Management for $47.75 million in 2002. The property spans 520,918 SF with rents ranging from $1,974 to $5,341 depending on unit size (795–1,554 SF). This represents TA Realty's second major South Florida multifamily investment in under 12 months and signals continued confidence in the market's value-add and rent-growth opportunity.
stories.impact: Strong pricing and repeat investment in South Florida communities indicate sustained investor appetite despite recent rate volatility; TA Realty's capital deployment (>$200M South Florida in 12 months) suggests stabilized financing and cap-rate clarity, reducing development underwriting uncertainty for competing projects in Wellington, Pembroke Pines, and greater Miami corridor.

stories.title: What Past Fed Hiking Cycles Signal for Yields, Recession Risk
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary The Federal Reserve’s quarter-point increase to a 3.75% to 4% target range began its first tightening campaign since July 2023, with policymakers signaling that at least one more increase may be needed before year-end. Past hiking cycles have ranged from modest adjustments to the aggressive inflation-fighting campaigns of the 1970s and early 1980s. Larger and faster cycles were more likely to precede recessions, although a recession was not inevitable. History offers no single answer. But it does show that the level of inflation, the pace of rate hikes, and the Treasury market’s response have been critical in determining whether a hiking cycle ends in a soft landing, a bond-market disruption or a recession. Inflation’s Historical Role The most aggressive tightening cycles occurred when inflation was already deeply embedded in the economy. From March 1972 through July 1974, the Fed raised its policy rate by roughly 930 basis points as CPI was running near 3.6% at the start of the cycle. The campaign overlapped with the recession that began in November 1973 and lasted 16 months. Long-term yields rose sharply as inflation accelerated, and the oil shock added to investor concern. The Fed’s next major campaign began in January 1977, when CPI was about 5.2%. Rates rose by roughly 1,300 basis points through April 1980. A recession began in January 1980 and lasted six months. The central bank resumed aggressive tightening in August 1980, with CPI near 12.9%. Rates rose another 1,000 basis points through June 1981. The recession that began a month later lasted 16 months, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed into the mid-teens as investors demanded greater compensation for inflation risk. Those periods illustrate the danger of allowing price pressures to become entrenched. Once inflation expectations rise, policymakers may need to tighten more forcefully, increasing the odds of a significant economic downturn. The 1983-84 cycle offered a different outcome.
bullets: Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4% in first tightening cycle since July 2023; signals more hikes possible by year-end
Historical analysis: larger/faster hiking cycles preceded recessions; 1972–74 cycle raised rates ~930 bps amid 3.6% inflation
Treasury market response and inflation pace critical variables determining soft landing vs. bond disruption or recession
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve has begun a new tightening campaign with a quarter-point rate increase to 3.75%–4% and signaled at least one more hike may occur before year-end. Historical precedent shows larger and faster tightening cycles are more likely to precede recessions, though outcomes depend on inflation levels, rate-hike speed, and Treasury market response. The 1972–74 cycle saw ~930 bps of rate increases with CPI near 3.6%, overlapping a 16-month recession; the 1977 campaign occurred at 5.2% inflation.
stories.impact: Rate trajectory uncertainty increases cost-of-capital risk for development underwriting and refinancing; multifamily sponsors should stress-test acquisition yields and construction financing assumptions against recession scenarios, particularly if Fed continues beyond market-expected terminal rate—cap-rate compression from 2023 lows may not hold if inflation re-accelerates and tightening extends.

stories.title: Piedmont Building $600M Covington Hospital
stories.excerpt: Piedmont plans to build a relocation hospital for Piedmont Newton Hospital, located in Covington, GA, at a cost of nearly $600 million, all of which will be borne by Piedmont. The existing hospital is licensed for 128 beds but is currently limited by its aging and landlocked physical plant. This will be the second-largest capital project in the organization’s history, after the Marcus Tower opened on its Piedmont Atlanta Hospital campus in 2020. In addition to this project, Piedmont has invested nearly $2 billion into expansion projects in the communities it serves over the past five years. Piedmont partnered with Newton Medical Center to form Piedmont Newton in 2015. Like many community and rural hospitals across the country at that time, Newton Medical Center had struggled to remain financially sustainable. Piedmont has since invested $70 million into expanding services in the community and into the hospital facility itself, which was built in 1954. Newton County is located 35 miles east of Atlanta. The post Piedmont Building $600M Covington Hospital appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Piedmont Hospital investing ~$600M to relocate Piedmont Newton Hospital in Covington, GA (35 mi east of Atlanta)
Existing 128-bed facility built 1954, landlocked; second-largest capital project in Piedmont history after 2020 Marcus Tower
Piedmont invested $2B across expansion projects in served communities over past 5 years; $70M prior Newton investment
stories.summary: Piedmont Healthcare plans a $600 million relocation hospital project for Piedmont Newton Hospital in Covington, Georgia, approximately 35 miles east of Atlanta. The existing facility, licensed for 128 beds, is constrained by its 1954 vintage and landlocked site. This represents the second-largest capital project in Piedmont's history and follows $70 million in prior expansion investments at Newton; Piedmont has deployed $2 billion across facility expansion in its service area over five years.
stories.impact: Major healthcare capital deployment signals strong population/service demand in exurban Atlanta (Covington, Newton County); this drives indirect multifamily demand through health-sector employment growth and population stabilization in secondary markets, creating potential value-add development windows for apartment communities near emerging hospital campuses in underpenetrated East Atlanta suburbs.

stories.title: 766K-SF Sarasota Cold Storage Facility Available for Lease
stories.excerpt: The former United Natural Foods distribution center at 6100 McIntosh Road in Sarasota is available for lease. The 766,579-square-foot space, representing approximately 82% of the 929,856-square-foot Gulf Coast Gateway building, includes 202,857 square feet of cold storage, believed to be the largest block of its kind that is available in the state. Nick DeVito II and Brie Tulp of Ian Black Real Estate, Lisa Ross and Trey Carswell, of Cushman & Wakefield, are the listing agents on the property. Agellan owns the building. Originally constructed by Winn-Dixie in 1981 for grocery distribution, the property has a long history as a major food logistics facility. Another value-add of the property is the adjacent IOS land. The space offers tenants additional space for trucks, trailers, equipment or other outdoor storage. Ross added, “The combination of significant cold storage capacity, dry warehouse space, existing specialized infrastructure and adjacent IOS creates a highly flexible solution for a wide range of users.” The post 766K-SF Sarasota Cold Storage Facility Available for Lease appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 766,579 SF former UNFI distribution center available for lease in Sarasota; 202,857 SF cold storage (largest block in FL)
Gulf Coast Gateway building (929,856 SF total); originally 1981 Winn-Dixie grocery facility; adjacent IOS land available
Agellan owns asset; CBRE and Ian Black Real Estate listing agents seek food logistics and specialized storage tenants
stories.summary: A 766,579-square-foot industrial space at 6100 McIntosh Road in Sarasota, representing 82% of the Gulf Coast Gateway building, is available for lease. The property includes 202,857 SF of cold storage—reportedly the largest contiguous block available in Florida—and was originally built by Winn-Dixie in 1981 for grocery distribution. Adjacent land and existing specialized infrastructure support flexible uses for logistics and food-distribution tenants.
stories.impact: Large-block cold-storage availability in Sarasota may signal softening in industrial occupancy or landlord repositioning, but supply-constrained cold-storage market suggests strong underlying demand fundamentals; for multifamily developers, logistics employment anchors in Sarasota-Bradenton support renter base, though capital flows to industrial cap rates may compete for equity in coastal Florida markets.

stories.title: Swickard Acquires 90% Stake in Portland’s Park Avenue West
stories.excerpt: Jeff Swickard, president and CEO of Swickard Group, has acquired a 90% interest in Park Avenue West, the fourth-largest building in downtown Portland and the latest prominent high-rise in his nearly $250 million investment in the city over the past year. Swickard’s commitment of more than $100 million for the majority interest in Park Avenue West represents another significant long-term investment in Portland. His other recent investments include the landmark U.S. Bancorp Tower, known as Big Pink, the Five Oak Building and BMW Portland in Goose Hollow. Park Avenue West, a 30-story tower across from Director Park and Nordstrom at 760 S.W. Ninth Ave., opened in 2016 with a mix of luxury apartments, office space and ground-floor retail, including Pendleton Woolen Mills. Swickard is investing alongside the existing owners of Park Avenue West, TMT Development and others, who will retain the remaining 10% interest. Swickard Group is a diversified investment and operating company with interests in automotive retail, real estate and hospitality. The post Swickard Acquires 90% Stake in Portland’s Park Avenue West appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Jeff Swickard acquires 90% stake in Park Avenue West (30-story, Portland, OR) for >$100M alongside TMT Development
2016-opened mixed-use tower (760 S.W. Ninth Ave): luxury apartments, office, retail; includes Pendleton Woolen Mills
Swickard invested ~$250M in Portland over past year; also acquired U.S. Bancorp Tower, Five Oak Building, BMW Portland
stories.summary: Jeff Swickard has acquired a 90% interest in Park Avenue West, a 30-story mixed-use tower in downtown Portland opened in 2016, representing more than $100 million of his recent $250 million Portland real estate investment commitment. The property at 760 S.W. Ninth Avenue includes luxury apartments, office space, and ground-floor retail anchored by Pendleton Woolen Mills. Swickard's other recent Portland acquisitions include the U.S. Bancorp Tower, Five Oak Building, and BMW Portland.
stories.impact: Single institutional investor (Swickard) deploying $250M into Portland downtown indicates confidence in market stabilization and value-creation opportunity; for multifamily, this signals potential repositioning of underperforming or distressed mixed-use assets and suggests cap-rate clarity sufficient to attract large-scale capital—competitive pressure may stiffen pricing on Portland apartment acquisitions in 2026.

stories.title: The C-PACE Opportunity for Ground-Leased Properties
stories.excerpt: Ground leases underlie some of the country’s most valuable commercial real estate. They are common in high-value markets such as Manhattan and are frequently used when land is owned by a university, public authority, institution or large corporate entity. They can also provide the long-term site control needed for projects involving new market tax credits or historical tax credits while allowing the landowner to retain fee ownership. Despite their widespread use, ground leases are often treated as an obstacle to efficient property financing. Lease provisions governing assignments, subletting, mortgages and ownership transfers can complicate a transaction. Mortgage lenders must also consider what happens to their collateral if the lease expires or is terminated. Michele Pitale. Credit: Courtesy CounterpointeSRE. Those concerns are legitimate, but they should not prevent an otherwise viable project from moving forward. Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing can serve as an effective solution. Ground-leased developments often have many of the same financing objectives as fee simple properties. Sponsors seek to preserve equity, lower the weighted average cost of capital, improve project cash flow, finance energy-related improvements over their useful life, and reduce refinancing risk through long-term, fixed-rate capital. C-PACE is typically fully amortizing with fixed rates over the long term, often up to 30 years. It can complement construction and permanent financing while improving the efficiency of the overall capital stack. Ground-leased properties face additional obstacles when seeking mortgage financing that C-PACE may be able to address. There are no financial covenants in C-PACE requiring explicit consent or approvals that restrict assignments, subletting, mortgaging or transferring ownership. bullets: C-PACE financing solution addresses ground-lease complications (assignments, mortgages, fee-simple barriers)
Common in high-value markets (Manhattan, universities, public authorities); long-term site control aids new market and historical tax credits
Mortgage lenders concern over lease expiration/termination and collateral risk; C-PACE preserves equity and lowers weighted-average cost
stories.summary: Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing offers a structured solution to financing challenges inherent in ground-leased properties, which are prevalent in high-value markets like Manhattan and properties owned by universities, public authorities, or institutions. Ground leases complicate traditional financing due to restrictions on assignments, subletting, mortgages, and ownership transfers, plus lender concerns about collateral at lease expiration. C-PACE allows sponsors to preserve equity and lower weighted-average cost of capital while maintaining long-term site control needed for new market and historical tax-credit projects.
stories.impact: C-PACE unlocks development feasibility for ground-leased projects in high-value urban markets; multifamily developers with ground-leased Manhattan or institutional-land sites can now model higher leverage and lower cost-of-capital, potentially unlocking marginal projects and increasing competitive intensity for scarce urban land parcels where fee-simple ownership is unavailable.

stories.title: The Plan: NYC’s First Flight Club Aims for a Bull’s-Eye at 31 Union Square West
stories.excerpt: The first rule of Flight Club is to find a historically significant building to lease. Founded in 2012 by British friends Steve Moore and Paul Barham, Flight Club — a U.K.-based chain of fanciful pubs for darts aficionados — has grown into an international event venue that brings people together with food, fun, drinks and, of course, darts. Flight Club, which State of Play Hospitality operates in North America under license, is getting ready to open its first New York City location — but 12th in the U.S. — at 31 Union Square West. Built between 1902 and 1903, 31 Union Square West was previously headquarters to the Bank of Metropolis, and then served as the home of the Blue Water Grill restaurant from 1996 to 2019. Commercial Observer A space with a unique history in an active restaurant and entertainment hub was key in the search for Flight Club’s first New York City spot. “The brand owners in the U.K. have always sought out historic, architecturally significant, beautiful buildings,” said Toby Harris, president and CEO of State of Play Hospitality. “That’s always been a pillar of the brand in the U.K., and it’s wonderful that we managed to find such a building in New York.” The Union Square West location is designed to reflect the overall Flight Club aesthetic. But its hoped-for clientele — a blend of corporate clients and social guests — will also encounter elements unique to that space due to the property’s vintage. “The building dates to the earliest days of the 20th century,” Harris said. “It’s a spectacular space, and we’ve tried to retain as many original features as possible, starting with the ground-floor banking hall that is blessed with the most wonderful, stunning marble on the walls, and some amazing mosaic tiles on the floor. bullets: Flight Club opens first NYC location (12th U.S.) at 31 Union Square West; U.K. darts-pub chain expanding in North America
Historic 1902–1903 building, formerly Bank of Metropolis, housed Blue Water Grill 1996–2019; active restaurant/entertainment district
State of Play Hospitality operates North American license; appeals to event/hospitality foot traffic and night-economy demand
stories.summary: Flight Club, a U.K.-based darts-themed pub and event venue founded in 2012, is opening its first New York City location (12th U.S.) at 31 Union Square West, a historically significant 1902–1903 building formerly housing the Bank of Metropolis and the Blue Water Grill restaurant (1996–2019). State of Play Hospitality operates the North American franchise. The venue combines food, drinks, and darts in a renovated historic space anchoring an active Manhattan entertainment district.
stories.impact: Ground-floor restaurant/hospitality leasing in Union Square signals ongoing recovery of NYC entertainment/night-economy demand post-pandemic; this supports multifamily renter demand in adjacent NoMad and Flatiron submarkets where young professionals cluster, validating neighborhood walkability and amenity density as lease-renewal factors.

stories.title: Distyl AI Doubles Its 135 Madison Offices to 30K SF After Less Than a Year
stories.excerpt: Software development company Distyl AI has room to grow. The artificial intelligence-powered developer of operating systems for large companies has leased the entire ninth floor at 135 Madison Avenue in Manhattan’s NoMad neighborhood, according to building manager Koeppel Rosen, bringing the company’s total footprint to 30,076 square feet. Distyl AI arrived at the Rosen family’s 13-story building in December 2025, Commercial Observer reported at the time, initially taking 15,038 square feet across the entire 10th floor. Asking rent for the recent expansion was $55 per square foot, and both leases run through January 2028, according to Crain’s New York Business, which first reported the lease. Koeppel Rosen’s Max Koeppel represented the Rosen family in the transaction, while Justin Pollner and Steven Rotter of Newmark negotiated on behalf of Distyl AI. Distyl AI’s arrival at 135 Madison in December represented the company’s first office in New York City and second location overall, after establishing its headquarters at 55 Hawthorne Street in San Francisco in 2022. “We were pleased to work with Distyl AI to reconfigure and expand its footprint across two contiguous floors at 135 Madison Avenue,” Koeppel said in a statement. “We celebrate the company’s rapidly growing operations, which required additional office space.” The office building on the corner of East 31st Street and Madison Avenue is also home to health care technology platform Courier Health, coworking firm WeWork, digital marketing firm Demand Growth Digital, e-commerce marketing company Mobikasa and event space provider Blender Workspace. A spokesperson for Distyl AI did not immediately respond to a requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Distyl AI (AI OS developer) expands 135 Madison Avenue footprint to 30,076 SF (doubled from 15,038 SF) in <1 year
Initial 10th floor (Dec 2025) + newly leased entire 9th floor; $55/SF asking rent; leases through Jan 2028
Company's NYC office established Dec 2025; HQ at 55 Hawthorne Street, San Francisco; rapid expansion signals hiring/growth
stories.summary: Distyl AI, an artificial intelligence-powered operating-systems developer, has doubled its Manhattan office footprint to 30,076 square feet by leasing the entire 9th floor of 135 Madison Avenue in NoMad, less than one year after establishing its first New York City office on the 10th floor in December 2025. The expansion lease was negotiated at $55 per square foot with both leases running through January 2028. The company maintains headquarters in San Francisco and uses its NYC presence as a second major office location.
stories.impact: Rapid tech-company office expansion (100% floor-space growth in <12 months) in Manhattan NoMad indicates strong hiring confidence and talent-market competition; this drives renter demand for nearby apartment stock (NoMad, Gramercy, Murray Hill) from mid-to-senior software engineers, supporting rent resilience and turnover demand in transit-proximate multifamily in East Midtown.

stories.title: CIP Real Estate Buys San Gabriel Valley Industrial Park for $61M
stories.excerpt: The owner of a 200,049-square-foot industrial and flex complex in Los Angeles County’s San Gabriel Valley has unloaded the asset for $60.7 million. The Irvine-based CIP Real Estate acquired the Walnut Tech Business Center, an 11-building property at Valley Boulevard and Lemon Avenue in Walnut, from an affiliate of AEW. The complex contains 109 industrial, flex-office and service-commercial suites ranging from 640 to 8,400 square feet and is 92 percent leased. Property records show City National Bank provided $42.9 million in acquisition financing, arranged by JLL. CIP also plans a $3.5 million capital improvement program this year. The business center sits about a mile from the 60 Freeway and serves the City of Industry area, where small bay industrial space remains highly supply constrained. “Very few quality small bay industrial parks come available for sale in Southern California each year, especially a best-in-class project in this strategically important submarket of L.A. County,” CIP CEO Eric Smyth said in a statement. CIP represented itself in the transaction, while JLL’s Patrick Nally, Evan Moran and Chad Solomon represented AEW. The Walnut acquisition extends a busy stretch for CIP. The firm said it has closed more than $200 million in industrial park transactions over the past 90 days across Dallas, South Florida and Atlanta, bringing its industrial portfolio to more than $2.5 billion. The company owns and manages more than 12 million square feet of real estate. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: CIP Real Estate acquires Walnut Tech Business Center (San Gabriel Valley, CA) for $60.7M from AEW affiliate
200,049 SF, 11 buildings, 109 suites (640–8,400 SF); 92% leased; $3.5M capex planned; City National Bank financed $42.9M
Walnut submarket near 60 Freeway, City of Industry; CIP CEO notes scarcity of quality small-bay industrial supply in LA County
stories.summary: CIP Real Estate purchased the Walnut Tech Business Center, an 11-building industrial and flex complex totaling 200,049 square feet in Walnut, California, from an AEW affiliate for $60.7 million. The property includes 109 industrial and flex-office suites ranging from 640 to 8,400 SF and is 92% leased. CIP secured $42.9 million in acquisition financing from City National Bank via JLL and plans a $3.5 million capital-improvement program. The location, one mile from the 60 Freeway, serves the supply-constrained City of Industry submarket.
stories.impact: Strong acquisition pricing and capital availability for supply-constrained small-bay industrial in Los Angeles County signals robust logistics and light-manufacturing employment fundamentals; sustained industrial job growth in City of Industry (adjacent to Walnut) supports population retention and renter demand in surrounding East LA County markets, favoring apartment developments near transit and employment centers.
